title: The fast God chooses (Isaiah 58:6–7)
hookLine: loosen the bands, share your bread, don't hide from your own flesh

lines: A QUESTION THAT TURNS IT INSIDE OUT.
cards: Everything done right. The meals skipped. The rough clothes on.
The head bowed all day. The whole routine, carefully kept, and nothing happens. So the complaint goes up, a little hurt: we fasted, God, and you didn't even notice.
The prophet Isaiah hears it from his people, and God's answer through him is blunt. You fast, and on the same day you're squeezing your workers. You fast, and you're picking fights.
Then comes a question that turns fasting inside out.

teach.h: WE FASTED, AND THOU SEEST NOT?
teach.b: In Isaiah fifty-eight, the people ask, in the King James Bible: "Wherefore have we fasted, say they, and thou seest not?" God answers with a different kind of fast.

teach.h: LOOSE THE BANDS, UNDO THE BURDENS.
teach.b: "Is not this the fast that I have chosen? to loose the bands of wickedness, to undo the heavy burdens, and to let the oppressed go free, and that ye break every yoke? Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house? when thou seest the naked, that thou cover him; and that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh?"
Fasting was about what you don't eat. Here, it's about who else gets to eat: your empty plate is supposed to become someone else's full one.

teach.h: DEAL THY BREAD TO THE HUNGRY.
teach.b: Isaiah isn't throwing out fasting; he's saying a fast that leaves the hungry hungry has missed the point.
And that last line, hide not thyself from thine own flesh: your own flesh means your own people, your family, your neighbor, the human being in front of you. Don't look away.

teach.h: THY LIGHT BREAK FORTH AS THE MORNING.
teach.b: And a promise: "Then shall thy light break forth as the morning." Jews read this chapter aloud on Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, right in the middle of the fast.
Christians lean on it too: in the custom of giving to the poor what you'd have spent on food during Lent, and in movements for justice that quoted Isaiah to the powerful.
The prophet asks every fast the same question: who got fed?

how: Many Christians pair fasting with giving, setting aside the money they would have spent on food during Lent or on fast days and giving it to the poor, often through church collections or food banks.

he redefines it: a fast should feed the hungry and free the oppressed.
Jews read Isaiah 58 on Yom Kippur
it's read aloud on the Day of Atonement, in the middle of the fast.
hide not thyself from thine own flesh means avoid temptation
it means don't look away from your own people: family, neighbor, the person in front of you.

games.q: you've fasted all day, carefully. you complain to God: we fasted, and you didn't notice. what does God answer through Isaiah?
o: share your bread with the hungry and set the oppressed free.
games.why: "is not this the fast that I have chosen?" not a longer fast, but one that feeds the hungry and loosens every yoke.

practice: Think of what you'll spend on yourself today that you could skip, a coffee out, a lunch, a delivery fee, a small treat, and put a number on it.

Picture where that money could go instead, a food bank, a neighbor who's short this month, the person asking for change outside the store, and, without guilt, let Isaiah's picture sit with you: your empty plate becoming someone's full one.
If you pray, pray for someone who is hungry today.
